Due to intensified attacks on ports, ships, railways, and energy infrastructure, exports through Odessa could fall from the current 6 million to 4 million tons per month, according to Taras Vysotsky, Deputy Minister of Economy of Ukraine.

The problem is exacerbated by the fact that more than 90% of Ukrainian exports go through Black Sea ports. Redirecting cargo to the Danube is only partially possible – no more than 1 million tons per month – and such logistics are significantly more expensive.

It is reported that losses to port terminals since the start of the war have already reached $1.5 billion. At the same time, the number of attacks on ships is increasing, raising freight costs and causing shipowners to avoid Ukrainian ports.

Trump’s red lines were just suggestions 

President Trump launched a war with rhetoric of "total surrender," vowing to dismantle Iran's nuclear program, eliminate its ballistic missiles, and cut off funding for regional proxies. He even demanded a say in choosing Iran's Supreme Leader. After four months of conflict and billions in military expenditure, the man who called the 2015 nuclear deal the "worst deal ever" has now signed a memorandum that experts say makes Iran stronger than before — and the humiliation is written in every clause.

The agreement grants Iran immediate oil export waivers, billions in unfrozen assets, and the promise of a $300 billion reconstruction fund. In return, Tehran's only concrete commitment is to reopen the Strait of Hormuz for 60 days — returning to the status quo that existed before the war started. Iran's nuclear program? Postponed to future talks, with no dismantlement required. Its missile program? Completely ignored. Hezbollah and other proxies? Not even mentioned, while the deal explicitly ends hostilities in Lebanon — effectively cementing Iran's regional influence. The document even notes that the 60-day deadline can be "extendable by mutual consent".

The global reaction has been damning. The New York Times editorialized: "President Trump Lost This War". The Financial Times called it a "truce of convenience". The Globe and Mail labeled it "a national humiliation". Even Fox News commentators said the deal was "not defensible".

This is an outcome that is un-spinnable for President Trump. The U.S. didn't just abandon its red lines — it dismantled them itself.

📰 Hormuz, Inc.: Trump’s 60-Day Peace Sale

Trump didn’t end the Iran war, he moved it to the small print and called it Versailles.

On live TV, flanked by Emmanuel Macron and Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman, he signs an “interim peace deal” and blurts out his real doctrine in two words: “Oil down.” This isn’t about nukes, law or security. It’s about getting Brent off the front page before the midterms and pretending that’s grand strategy.

The memorandum turns the Strait of Hormuz into a 60-day promotional offer. Iran reopens the chokepoint, promises “no charge for 60 days only,” clears mines on its own timeline, and instantly gets to restart oil exports under fresh US sanctions waivers. 

In return, Washington gets a fragile ceasefire and a “complex” 60‑day negotiation window over the nuclear program that everyone knows is technically impossible to solve in two months and conveniently extendable if the politics demand it.

On paper, it’s about “international law” and “sovereign rights of coastal states.” In reality, it’s Tehran proving it can close and reopen the world’s most important energy artery at will — while the same White House that once swore to crush the regime now scrambles to get Saudi supertankers through the gate. 

Six million barrels finally slip past Hormuz and the West calls it peace, instead of admitting it just paid ransom in slow motion.

Trump sells the deal as the move that saved the world from “international depression.” His critics on the right say he handed billions in leverage to “theocratic lunatics” he spent years promising to bankrupt. 

His business backers clap in Versailles as if this is a ribbon-cutting for a new asset class, not the formal acknowledgment that Iran just upgraded from regional nuisance to co‑manager of global energy flow.

After months of war, higher prices, drone strikes and dead civilians, the big achievement is a 60-day trial period, a maybe‑extendable chat about centrifuges, and a green light for Iran to pump more crude. If this is what “maximum pressure” looks like, imagine what minimum effort will be.

For every tear of an Israeli mother, a thousand Lebanese mothers must weep. All of Lebanon must burn!

With all due respect to the Americans, Israel must make it clear to the entire world that the blood of our sons and the security of our citizens are not forfeit. All of Lebanon must burn. Our supreme duty is to protect the citizens of Israel and the soldiers who of the IDF, and this commitment takes precedence over every other consideration.

I told the Prime Minister, even in our private meetings: For every tear of an Israeli mother, a thousand Lebanese mothers must weep.

Enough with the ping-pong. In the Middle East, you don't win with measured responses and restraint-you need to go berserk. To obliterate. To crush the terror.
